segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Here, one of the show's judges, Michelle Ogunderhin, tells BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour why she thinks clutter is such a problem.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Visual clutter is more exhausting than we realise. It's not just stuff. Our brains are constantly processing our surroundings, so they have to work overtime if they're surrounded by chaos.
segments.fa: شلوغی بصری خسته‌کننده‌تر از اونیه که فکر می‌کنیم. فقط اشیاء نیست. مغز ما مدام محیط اطرافش رو پردازش می‌کنه، پس اگه دور و برش آشوب باشه، مجبوره اضافه کار کنه.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So if you feel drained or exhausted at home, it could be your clutter.

segments.text: In a cluttered room our brains work overtime

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: meaning they work extra hard to make sense of the disorder,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: leaving us exhausted.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So why do many of us find it hard to throw stuff away, even things we rarely use?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Plus, it can be emotionally disturbing deciding what to keep and what to throw away.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: But don't worry, says professional organiser and host of the Declutter Club podcast, Ingrid Janssen.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: The answer is to go slow, as she explains here to BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: You have to do decluttering slowly but surely. One drawer, one cupboard at a time. You can't go in all guns blazing. You can't go in, that's what we hear all the time, this weekend I'm going to sort out my whole room of doom.

segments.text: When it comes to decluttering your home, it's best to do things slowly but surely,
